history.heading: Portuguese Timor
paragraphs: Timor-Leste (East Timor) occupies the eastern half of the island of Timor, plus the enclave of Oecusse and nearby islands. Austronesian and Melanesian peoples lived in small kingdoms that traded sandalwood. Portuguese traders and missionaries arrived in the 16th century, and Portugal colonised the eastern part, while the Dutch took the west, which became part of Indonesia.

history.heading: Indonesian occupation
paragraphs: After Portugal's 1974 revolution, Timor-Leste declared independence in November 1975, but Indonesia invaded days later and annexed it. The occupation was brutal: up to a quarter of the population, around 100,000 to 180,000 people, died from violence, hunger and disease. The 1991 Santa Cruz massacre in Dili drew international attention. Bishop Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1996.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: In a UN-organised referendum in 1999, nearly 80 percent voted for independence. Indonesian-backed militias responded with widespread destruction. After a UN administration, Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002, the first new state of the 21st century. Resistance leader Xanana Gusmão has been president and prime minister. Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in October 2025.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Tetum and Portuguese are official languages, and Indonesian and English are working languages. Over 95 percent of people are Catholic, one of the highest shares in the world. Tais, handwoven textiles, are recognised by UNESCO. Traditional sacred houses (uma lulik) are central to community life.

politics.heading: Semi-presidential democracy
paragraphs: Timor-Leste is a semi-presidential republic and one of the freest democracies in Southeast Asia. Leaders of the resistance generation, such as Gusmão and Ramos-Horta, still dominate politics. It has resolved maritime boundary disputes with Australia.

economy.heading: Oil and the future
paragraphs: Timor-Leste depends heavily on revenues from offshore oil and gas, saved in a Petroleum Fund, but existing fields are running out. Developing the Greater Sunrise gas field is a national priority. Most people work in subsistence farming, and coffee is the main non-oil export. Poverty and malnutrition remain high. The currency is the US dollar.
